{{Short description|Mathematical model for state estimation}}
In the theory of [[stochastic processes]], '''filtering''' describes the problem of determining the [[State (controls)|state]] of a system from an incomplete and potentially [[Noise (signal processing)|noisy]] set of observations. For example, in [[GPS navigation]], filtering helps estimate a car’s true position (the state) from noisy satellite signals (the observations). While originally motivated by problems in engineering, filtering found applications in many fields from signal processing to finance.

The problem of optimal non-linear filtering (even for the non-stationary case) was solved by [[Ruslan L. Stratonovich]] (1959,<ref>[[Ruslan_Stratonovich|Stratonovich, R. L.]] (1959). ''Optimum nonlinear systems which bring about a separation of a signal with constant parameters from noise''. Radiofizika, 2:6, pp. 892-901.</ref> 1960<ref>Stratonovich, R.L. (1960). ''Application of the Markov processes theory to optimal filtering''. Radio Engineering and Electronic Physics, 5:11, pp.1-19.</ref>), see also [[Harold J. Kushner]]'s work <ref>[[Harold_J._Kushner|Kushner, Harold]]. (1967). Nonlinear filtering: The exact dynamical equations satisfied by the conditional mode. Automatic Control, IEEE Transactions on Volume 12, Issue 3, Jun 1967 Page(s): 262 - 267</ref> and [[Moshe Zakai]]'s, who introduced a simplified dynamics for the unnormalized conditional law of the filter<ref>[[Moshe_Zakai|Zakai, Moshe]] (1969), On the optimal filtering of diffusion processes. Zeit. Wahrsch. 11  230–243. {{MR|242552}}, {{Zbl|0164.19201}}, {{doi|10.1007/BF00536382}}</ref> known as the [[Zakai equation]].  The solution, however, is infinite-dimensional in the general case.<ref name=Michel>Mireille Chaleyat-Maurel and Dominique Michel. Des resultats de non existence de filtre de dimension finie. Stochastics, 13(1+2):83-102, 1984.</ref> Certain approximations and special cases are well understood: for example, the linear filters are optimal for Gaussian random variables, and are known as the [[Wiener filter]] and the [[Kalman-Bucy filter]]. More generally, as the solution is infinite dimensional, it requires finite dimensional approximations to be implemented in a computer with finite memory. A finite dimensional approximated [[nonlinear filter]] may be more based on heuristics, such as the [[extended Kalman filter]] or the [[assumed density filter]]s,<ref>Maybeck, Peter S., Stochastic models, estimation, and control, Volume 141, Series Mathematics in Science and Engineering, 1979, Academic Press</ref> or more methodologically oriented such as for example the [[projection filters]],<ref>[[Damiano Brigo]], Bernard Hanzon and François LeGland, A Differential Geometric approach to nonlinear filtering: the Projection Filter, I.E.E.E. Transactions on Automatic Control Vol. 43, 2 (1998), pp 247--252.</ref> some sub-families of which are shown to coincide with the assumed density filters.<ref>Damiano Brigo, Bernard Hanzon and François Le Gland, Approximate Nonlinear Filtering by Projection on Exponential Manifolds of Densities, Bernoulli, Vol. 5, N. 3 (1999), pp. 495--534</ref> 
[[Particle filter]]s<ref name=":22">{{cite journal|last1 = Del Moral|first1 = Pierre|title = Measure Valued Processes and Interacting Particle Systems. Application to Non Linear Filtering Problems|journal = Annals of Applied Probability|date = 1998|edition = Publications du Laboratoire de Statistique et Probabilités, 96-15 (1996)|volume = 8|issue = 2|pages = 438–495|url = http://projecteuclid.org/download/pdf_1/euclid.aoap/1028903535|doi = 10.1214/aoap/1028903535|doi-access = free|url-access = subscription}}</ref> are another option to attack the infinite dimensional filtering problem and are based on   sequential Monte Carlo methods.

In general, if the [[separation principle]] applies, then filtering also arises as part of the solution of an [[optimal control]] problem. For example, the [[Kalman filter]] is the estimation part of the optimal control solution to the [[linear-quadratic-Gaussian control]] problem.

==The mathematical formalism==

Consider a [[probability space]] (Ω,&nbsp;Σ,&nbsp;'''P''') and suppose that the (random) state ''Y''<sub>''t''</sub> in ''n''-[[dimension]]al [[Euclidean space]] '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> of a system of interest at time ''t'' is a [[random variable]] ''Y''<sub>''t''</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;Ω&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> given by the solution to an [[Kiyoshi Itō|Itō]] [[stochastic differential equation]] of the form

:<math>\mathrm{d} Y_{t} = b(t, Y_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} t + \sigma (t, Y_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} B_{t},</math>

where ''B'' denotes standard ''p''-dimensional [[Brownian motion]], ''b''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;+∞)&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> is the drift field, and ''σ''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;+∞)&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''&times;''p''</sup> is the diffusion field. It is assumed that observations ''H''<sub>''t''</sub> in '''R'''<sup>''m''</sup> (note that ''m'' and ''n'' may, in general, be unequal) are taken for each time ''t'' according to

:<math>H_{t} = c(t, Y_{t}) + \gamma (t, Y_{t}) \cdot \mbox{noise}.</math>

Adopting the Itō interpretation of the stochastic differential and setting

:<math> Z_{t} = \int_{0}^{t} H_{s} \, \mathrm{d} s,</math>

this gives the following stochastic integral representation for the observations ''Z''<sub>''t''</sub>:

:<math>\mathrm{d} Z_{t} = c(t, Y_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} t + \gamma (t, Y_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} W_{t},</math>

where ''W'' denotes standard ''r''-dimensional [[Brownian motion]], independent of ''B'' and the initial condition ''Y''<sub>0</sub>, and ''c''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;+∞)&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>  and ''γ''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;+∞)&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''&times;''r''</sup>  satisfy

:<math>\big| c (t, x) \big| + \big| \gamma (t, x) \big| \leq C \big( 1 + | x | \big)</math>

for all ''t'' and ''x'' and some constant ''C''.

The '''filtering problem''' is the following: given observations ''Z''<sub>''s''</sub> for 0&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''s''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''t'', what is the best estimate ''Ŷ''<sub>''t''</sub> of the true state ''Y''<sub>''t''</sub> of the system based on those observations?

By "based on those observations" it is meant that ''Ŷ''<sub>''t''</sub> is [[measurable function|measurable]] with respect to the [[sigma algebra|''&sigma;''-algebra]] ''G''<sub>''t''</sub> generated by the observations ''Z''<sub>''s''</sub>, 0&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''s''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''t''. Denote by ''K''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''K''(''Z'',&nbsp;''t'') the collection of all '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>-valued random variables ''Y'' that are square-integrable and ''G''<sub>''t''</sub>-measurable:

:<math>K = K(Z, t) = L^{2} (\Omega, G_{t}, \mathbf{P}; \mathbf{R}^{n}).</math>

By "best estimate", it is meant that ''Ŷ''<sub>''t''</sub> minimizes the mean-square distance between ''Y''<sub>''t''</sub> and all candidates in ''K'':

:<math>\mathbf{E} \left[ \big| Y_{t} - \hat{Y}_{t} \big|^{2} \right] = \inf_{Y \in K} \mathbf{E} \left[ \big| Y_{t} - Y \big|^{2} \right]. \qquad \mbox{(M)}</math>

==Basic result: orthogonal projection==

The space ''K''(''Z'',&nbsp;''t'') of candidates is a [[Hilbert space]], and the general theory of Hilbert spaces implies that the solution ''Ŷ''<sub>''t''</sub> of the minimization problem (M) is given by

:<math>\hat{Y}_{t} = P_{K(Z, t)} \big( Y_{t} \big),</math>

where ''P''<sub>''K''(''Z'',''t'')</sub> denotes the [[orthogonal projection]] of ''L''<sup>2</sup>(Ω,&nbsp;Σ,&nbsp;'''P''';&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>) onto the [[linear subspace]] ''K''(''Z'',&nbsp;''t'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''L''<sup>2</sup>(Ω,&nbsp;''G''<sub>''t''</sub>,&nbsp;'''P''';&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>). Furthermore, it is a general fact about [[conditional expectation]]s that if ''F'' is any sub-''σ''-algebra of Σ then the orthogonal projection

:<math>P_{K} : L^{2} (\Omega, \Sigma, \mathbf{P}; \mathbf{R}^{n}) \to  L^{2} (\Omega, F, \mathbf{P}; \mathbf{R}^{n})</math>

is exactly the conditional expectation operator '''E'''[·|''F''], i.e.,

:<math>P_{K} (X) = \mathbf{E} \big[ X \big | F \big].</math>

Hence,

:<math>\hat{Y}_{t} = P_{K(Z, t)} \big( Y_{t} \big) = \mathbf{E} \big[ Y_{t} \big | G_{t} \big].</math>

This elementary result is the basis for the general Fujisaki-Kallianpur-Kunita equation of filtering theory.

==More advanced result: nonlinear filtering SPDE==  
The complete knowledge of the filter at a time ''t'' would be given by the probability law of the signal ''Y''<sub>''t''</sub> conditional on the sigma-field ''G''<sub>''t''</sub> generated by observations ''Z'' up to time ''t''. If this probability law admits a density, informally 
:<math> p_t(y)\ dy = {\bf P}(Y_t \in dy|G_t), </math>
then under some regularity assumptions the density <math>p_t(y)</math> satisfies a non-linear [[stochastic partial differential equation]] (SPDE) driven by <math>dZ_t</math> and called [[Kushner_equation|Kushner-Stratonovich equation]],<ref name=BainCrisan>Bain, A., and Crisan, D. (2009). Fundamentals of Stochastic Filtering. Springer-Verlag, New York, 
 https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-76896-0</ref> or a unnormalized version <math>q_t(y)</math> of the density <math>p_t(y)</math> satisfies a linear SPDE called [[Zakai equation]].<ref name=BainCrisan /> 
These equations can be formulated for the above system, but to simplify the exposition one can assume that the unobserved signal ''Y'' and the partially observed noisy signal ''Z'' satisfy the equations 
:<math>\mathrm{d} Y_{t} = b(t, Y_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} t + \sigma (t, Y_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} B_{t},</math>
:<math>\mathrm{d} Z_{t} = c(t, Y_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} t +   \mathrm{d} W_{t}.</math>

In other terms, the system is simplified by assuming that the observation noise ''W'' is not state dependent. 
 
One might keep a deterministic time dependent <math>\gamma</math> in front of <math> dW</math> but we assume this has been taken out by re-scaling. 

For this particular system, the Kushner-Stratonovich SPDE for the density <math>p_t</math> reads
:<math>
\mathrm{d} p_t = {\cal L}^*_t  p_t \  dt 
+ p_t[c(t,\cdot) - E_{p_t}(c(t,\cdot))]^T [ d Z_t - E_{p_t}(c(t,\cdot)) d t]
</math>
where ''T'' denotes transposition, <math>E_p</math> denotes the expectation with respect to the density ''p'',   
<math> E_p[f] = \int f(y) p(y) dy,</math> 
and the forward diffusion operator <math>{\cal L}^*_t</math> is   
:<math>
{\cal L}_t^* f(t,y) = - \sum_i \frac{\partial}{\partial y_i} [ b_i(t,y) f(t,y) ] + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial y_i \partial y_j} [a_{ij}(t,y) f(t,y)]
</math>
where <math>a=\sigma \sigma^T</math>.
If we choose the unnormalized density <math> q_t(y)</math>, the Zakai SPDE for the same system reads
:<math>
\mathrm{d} q_t = {\cal L}^*_t  q_t \  dt 
+ q_t[c(t,\cdot)]^T  d Z_t .
</math>
These SPDEs for ''p'' and ''q'' are written in Ito calculus form. It is possible to write them in Stratonovich calculus form, which turns out to be helpful when deriving filtering approximations based on [[differential geometry]], as in the projection filters.
For example, the Kushner-Stratonovich equation written in Stratonovich calculus reads
:<math>   d p_t = {\cal L}^\ast_t\, p_t\,dt
   - \frac{1}{2}\, p_t\, [\vert c(\cdot, t) \vert^2 - E_{p_t}(\vert c(\cdot, t) \vert^2)] \,dt
   +  p_t\, [c(\cdot, t)-E_{p_t}(c(\cdot, t)) ]^T \circ dZ_t\ .</math>
From any of the densities ''p'' and ''q''  one can calculate all statistics of the signal ''Y''<sub>''t''</sub> conditional on the sigma-field generated by observations ''Z'' up to time ''t'', so that the densities give complete knowledge of the filter. Under the particular linear-constant assumptions with respect to ''Y'', where the systems coefficients ''b'' and ''c'' are linear functions of ''Y'' and where <math>\sigma</math> and <math>\gamma</math> do not depend on ''Y'', with the [[initial condition]] for the signal ''Y'' being Gaussian or deterministic, the density <math>p_t(y)</math> is Gaussian and it can be characterized by its mean and variance-covariance matrix, whose evolution is described by the [[Kalman_filter#Kalman–Bucy_filter|Kalman-Bucy filter]], which is finite dimensional.<ref name=BainCrisan /> More generally, the evolution of the filter density occurs in an infinite-dimensional [[function space]],<ref name=Michel /> and it has to be approximated via a finite dimensional approximation, as hinted above.
